claims.text: Enhanced Al–Ni short-range ordering promotes the formation of partial B2 ordering domains.
Partial B2 ordering stabilizes the bcc phase relative to the fcc phase in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloys.
Al–Ni SRO and associated B2 ordering govern phase stability in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys.
The proposed SRO-mediated phase stabilization is key to retaining high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness.
Casting or solution annealing can produce an Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloy with a mixed fcc and bcc microstructure.
Changing quench rates and aging times can systematically vary Al–Ni SRO without changing overall alloy composition.
Heat-treatment-induced localized Al–Ni SRO lowers the free energy of the bcc phase through B2-like ordering.
Lowering the bcc free energy relative to the fcc free energy shifts phase equilibrium toward a greater bcc fraction.
Samples with greater Al–Ni SRO will have a greater fraction or stability of the bcc/B2 phase than the baseline.
Greater Al–Ni SRO and bcc/B2 stabilization will enhance high-temperature strength.
Greater Al–Ni SRO and bcc/B2 stabilization will improve radiation tolerance.
Greater Al–Ni SRO and bcc/B2 stabilization will improve corrosion resistance.
Greater Al–Ni SRO and bcc/B2 stabilization will maintain or improve cryogenic toughness.
A conventional heat treatment produces a balanced fcc/bcc baseline with minimal targeted Al–Ni SRO enhancement.
Prior evidence links thermodynamic phase stability and phase fractions to mechanical response.
HEAs can display high-temperature strength and room- or cryogenic-temperature strength, ductility, and toughness.
Synchrotron XRD can be used to quantify the bcc phase fraction in the proposed samples.
Diffuse scattering and atom probe tomography can quantify or detect partial B2 ordering and Al–Ni SRO in the proposed samples.
